t: Card Flipping Game — One Observation Editorial
o:
## Understanding the problem

Each card shows one of its two numbers face up; we may flip any subset of cards. A value `x` is **good** if after our flips `x` is face down somewhere but face up nowhere. We want the minimum good value, or 0.

**Example 1:** fronts = [1,2,4,4,7], backs = [1,3,4,1,3]. Card 0 has 1 on both sides — it will *always* show 1, so 1 can never be good. Every other value (2,3,4,7) appears on only one side of each card it touches, so we can arrange flips so it is down everywhere. The minimum such value is **2**.

**Example 2:** fronts = [1], backs = [1]. The single card always shows 1, so nothing can be good → answer **0**.

With n ≤ 1000 and values ≤ 2000, even checking all values × cards ($O(n \cdot V)$) is fine; the key is realizing which values are impossible.
k: A value x is impossible to be good exactly when some card has x printed on BOTH sides — that card must show x forever.
For any other value x, we can flip cards independently so x ends up face down on one card and face up nowhere.
The answer is simply the minimum value among all numbers printed on the cards that never appear on both sides of the same card.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force over candidate values
a.i: Collect every distinct value that appears on any side. For each candidate x, check whether some card has x on both sides; if so, skip it. Otherwise x is achievable: flip every card whose current up-face equals x (making x down), and leave other cards alone — then x is down somewhere and up nowhere. Take the minimum valid candidate.
s: Build a set S of all values in fronts and backs.
Build a set B of 'bad' values: those with fronts[i] == backs[i] for some i.
Answer = min(S - B), or 0 if empty.
a.t: O(n) time — two linear passes with hash-set lookups.
a.sp: O(n) space for the hash sets of bad values.

a.n: Approach 2: Single pass without collecting candidates
a.i: Same insight, but instead of building a full candidate set first, do one pass to record bad values, then a second pass scanning both arrays for the minimum non-bad value. This avoids allocating a large union set and is marginally more memory-friendly.
s: Pass 1: insert fronts[i] into a set whenever fronts[i] == backs[i].
Pass 2: track min of fronts[i]/backs[i] not present in the set.
a.t: O(n) time — constant number of linear scans.
a.sp: O(n) worst case for the bad-value set (often much smaller).

w:
## Wrap-up

Both approaches share the same core observation; Approach 2 is the cleanest to present in an interview. **Why the insight holds:** flipping decisions per card are independent. If x never sits on both sides of one card, orient each card containing x so x faces down — x is now down somewhere and up nowhere. If x does sit on both sides of some card, that card permanently shows x, blocking x from ever being good.

**Pitfalls:**
- Don't require x to be absent from *all* fronts — x may appear on many fronts as long as each such card can be flipped.
- Remember to consider values from **both** arrays as candidates, not just backs.
- Return 0 when no candidate survives (e.g., every card is double-printed).

**Edge cases:** n = 1 with equal sides → 0; all cards identical doubles → 0; answer may come from a front value.

**Follow-ups:** What if you wanted the *maximum* good integer? (Same check, take max.) What if flips were limited to k cards? (Then the independence argument breaks and you'd need a different analysis.)
